# Conclusion  {#sec-discussion-outlook}

## Summary
Returning to the three questions posed in the introduction: demand is highly concentrated
in space and time. Downtown (the Loop and Near North Side) accounts for over 40 % of pickups
and O'Hare for a further 21 %, while the daily cycle runs from near zero overnight to a peak
around 17:00 (@sec-data-analytics). Community areas are the spatial unit best suited for fleet
management, being complete, free of interpolation artefacts, and small enough (roughly three
square miles) to act on, whereas census tracts are too sparse and privacy-suppressed to trust.
At this resolution, demand can be predicted well from calendar, weather, and location alone:
the feed-forward neural network reaches an R² of 0.90-0.93 and at the recommended
4-hour/community-area resolution, cuts the error of a naive historical-average baseline
by roughly 18 % (nMAE 0.25 against 0.31, @sec-demand-prediction). The additional complexity
of the deep learning approach is therefore justified, as unlike the SVR it can train on the
full multi-million-row dataset and stays stable at finer resolutions where the SVR degrades.
Lastly, home charging of an EV taxi can be optimized with reinforcement learning. A tabular
Monte Carlo agent cuts charging cost by about 50 % against a naive full-charge baseline while
keeping energy shortfalls to 0.14 % of episodes (@sec-rl). It is also the more practical
choice here, matching or exceeding a Deep Q-Network while being far easier and cheaper to
train, particularly during hyperparameter search, an advantage that holds only as long as
the state and action spaces stay small within the tabular agent's reach. 

## Discussion & Limitations
For the fleet operator, these results translate into concrete operational guidance.
The network's community-area, 4-hour forecasts are precise enough to steer vehicle
pre-positioning: supply should be concentrated at airports and downtown, with active
rebalancing back from the airport given its pickup-heavy asymmetry, and buffered
ahead of the evening peak and around weekends and holidays, where the demand *level*
shifts but not its *geography*. On charging, the RL results show that optimizing the at home
charging using smart agents has a high benefit in case of an exponential cost structure where
high charging power costs more as the operator directly controls timing and can shift power to
the cheapest, lowest-power slots. 

Still, there are multiple limitations to consider. On the trip data side, the demand models does not include the exact year and date to avoid overfitting but this prevents the models to learn a multi-year trend such as rising trip volumes in growing areas. Capturing this would require adding the feature back deliberately or retraining the model regularly as new data arrives. The point-of-interest features are static snapshots that cannot reflect how the POI landscape changes over time, a limitation we accept because static POIs still help the model relate similar areas to one another. The census tract layer is constrained by Chicago's privacy suppression, which strips tract information from low-frequency trips and affects more than half of all records. Further tract boundaries may have shifted within the observation window influencing the prediction. These two conditions mean that many temporal-spatial buckets were filled with zeros, which improves model fit but is a modelling convenience rather than ground truth. Coordinates throughout are area centroids rather than exact GPS points, so no encoding recovers true spatial precision beyond the community area or census tract. Model-side, the SVR's quadratic scaling meant it never saw more than a 50,000-row sample, so part of its gap to the network reflects data availability rather than architecture alone. The NN's own depth search, was run once on a baseline configuration rather than per experiment, due to compute constraints. On the RL side, the agent was trained on very specific environment settings for a fixed home-charging window with a fixed cost function and demand distribution, so it is not yet validated against fleet-scale coordination of many vehicles or real time-of-use electricity tariffs. Also it does not include public charging, which is likely if a driver is on a long trip or has to wait at the airport. The agent is also not yet validated against fleet-scale coordination of many vehicles or real time-of-use electricity tariffs.


## Future Work
Three directions would most improve the pilot's next iteration. First, moving the SVR to a linearly-scaling method, such as a gradient-boosted tree like XGBoost, which would allow it to train on the full dataset and also makes the results more explainable. Further it might be a fairer benchmark against the network, while an independent architecture search per neural network configuration would tighten that side of the comparison. Second, enriching the feature set with a genuine time trend and dynamic POI data, alongside external sources such as scheduled events (excluded here for incomplete timestamps) and public transit disruptions. Third, the smart charging agent should be extended from a single vehicle to a fleet-level setting with shared charging infrastructure, variable tariffs, and vehicle-specific battery, route profiles and more. This would be closer to a real-world scenario for a ride-hailing platform. This would then also influence the choice of learner, the state and action space grows and Monte Carlos or other tabular agents would most likely lose in comparison.
